title: Query optimisation: cost estimation
lead: Catalog statistics, selectivity formulas, join cardinality and histograms.

sections.title: Cost and cardinality statistics
sections.html:
A plan’s cost depends on the cost and output size of every operator. An intermediate result becomes the next operator’s input, so cardinality-estimation errors can change subsequent join and memory decisions.

Catalog statistics include NTuples, NPages, minimum/maximum values, distinct-value counts NKeys and index height. They are refreshed periodically, so estimates can be approximate or stale. The source’s System R model combines page I/Os and a weighted tuple-processing term.

Selectivity is output cardinality divided by input cardinality, between zero and one. A “highly selective” predicate in ordinary usage usually has a small numeric selectivity. Estimated output pages additionally depend on tuple width and packing.

PDF pp. 1–5

sections.title: Predicate selectivity
sections.html:
Under uniformity, equality to an existing value of A has estimated selectivity 1/V(A), where V(A) is its distinct count. For integer values uniformly covering [L,H], A > a has selectivity approximately (H − a)/(H − L + 1), clamped to the valid range.

For independent predicates, sel(P AND Q) ≈ sel(P)·sel(Q), and sel(P OR Q) ≈ sel(P) + sel(Q) − sel(P)·sel(Q). The general union formula subtracts the actual intersection; independence supplies the product approximation.

sel(NOT P) = 1 − sel(P) assumes two-valued predicates over the population being estimated. SQL NULL/UNKNOWN and correlated attributes require additional treatment. These formulas are modelling assumptions, not identities for arbitrary real data.

PDF pp. 6–9

sections.title: Join cardinality
sections.html:
For a non-null foreign key in S referencing a unique key in R, each S tuple has exactly one R match, so |R ⋈ S| = |S|. Nullable or unenforced foreign keys can reduce the inner-join result.

For a general equijoin on A, a common estimate is |R|·|S| / max(V(R.A), V(S.A)). It assumes uniform frequencies and containment of the smaller distinct-value domain in the larger one. Duplicate frequencies and partial domain overlap can violate the estimate.

Without adequate statistics, optimisers use defaults. Uniform estimates can be poor on skewed data; histograms retain more distribution information to improve estimates.

PDF pp. 10–14

sections.title: Equi-width and equi-depth histograms
sections.html:
A histogram divides an attribute’s domain into intervals and stores counts and boundaries. Equi-width buckets have equal value-range widths; equi-depth buckets contain approximately equal tuple counts and therefore use narrower ranges in dense regions.

Equality estimation distributes a bucket’s frequency across its represented values or distinct-value count. Range estimation sums full covered buckets and estimates the covered fraction of boundary buckets. Uniformity is still assumed inside each bucket.

More buckets increase resolution and catalog space. Histograms address single-attribute skew but do not by themselves establish independence between different attributes. The source’s plots compare how the two bucket schemes allocate resolution.

PDF pp. 15–26

quiz.question: An equi-width bucket contains 4 values and 60 rows. What is the estimated equality count for one value?
quiz.explanation: Assuming uniformity within the bucket gives 60/4=15. This is an estimate based on equal frequencies, not the actual count if the data is skewed.
